turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Mr. Hale, in you come. This is about the back, correct? We'll make it quick.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): It's nothing, really. Just a little sore. Carla's the one who dragged me in.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He winces getting out of the truck and then swears he's fine.
[SEG0004] person_1 (DOCTOR): How long has the pain been there.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): A few weeks. Or since the move. Don't ask me the date, I couldn't tell you. I don't track it.
[SEG0006] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was already hurting before the move. Early April. Two months, easy.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Two months, a few weeks, I don't—
[SEG0008] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): You do too know it's been longer. You complained packing the plates.
[SEG0009] person_1 (DOCTOR): So somewhere between a few weeks and two months, we'll leave it there. One side or the middle.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): Low back, middle, kicks left if I lift a box wrong. Dull, maybe a three out of ten. I'm not making a thing of it.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Does it shoot down the leg.
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Stays in the back.
[SEG0013] person_1 (DOCTOR): Numbness or tingling, feet or legs.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): Nope.
[SEG0015] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His right foot goes dead on the drive. He was shaking it out yesterday in the truck.
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the boot on the clutch. Sometimes it tingles, not really. I'm telling you it's nothing.
[SEG0017] person_1 (DOCTOR): Leg weak? Give out?
[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Hauled a dresser up Saturday. Legs are fine.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any trouble with the bladder. Can't start, leaking, can't empty.
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I pee normal. Gas station coffee has me in there a lot, that's the coffee, not this.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): Bowels different?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Same old.
[SEG0023] person_1 (DOCTOR): Unplanned weight loss.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Mm, I suppose. Belt's a little looser. But we've been on salads, so sometimes, not really.
[SEG0025] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He also skips—
[SEG0026] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'm not calling that weight loss. Any fever or chills.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever, no chills. Dock's hot so I sweat at work, that's the building.
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Wake you at night?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): A twinge if I roll over. Mornings are stiff, then once I'm moving on the warehouse floor it eases off.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Medicines. What do you take for the pain.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): Hang on, the stiff part is only like twenty minutes, then I'm good.
[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): Anyway, ibuprofen for the back, four hundred milligram tablets, by mouth, two maybe three times a day on long shifts.
[SEG0033] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He takes two of those at a pop, that's eight hundred milligrams, I've watched him. And he skips a bunch, then doubles up.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): One. Sometimes two, I don't sit there counting. Most days I take them. It's fine.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Naproxen, Tylenol, anything else.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Naproxen, the two hundred twenty milligram ones, I tried for about a week and my stomach burned, so I quit. There were little yellow pills from urgent care too, never got the name, they made me loopy and I stopped those.
[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I did steal one of Carla's headache pills one night. Waste of time.
[SEG0038] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): That was my sumatriptan. Not his, and he knows it.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): Drug allergies.
[SEG0040] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None.
[SEG0041] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Penicillin. Rash as a kid, his mother told me years ago. He pretends it didn't happen.
[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't buy that story. No allergies. I've taken whatever they hand me.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Back surgery ever.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): No. Never. Threw it out five-ish years ago, missed two days, done.
[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): Smoke? Alcohol?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Quit cigarettes five-ish years ago. One beer after work most nights. That's it.
[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Job?
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Warehouse, outbound at the distribution center. Boxes all day. Not quitting over this.
[SEG0049] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His father had two back surgeries. Before you say it doesn't matter—
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): Dad's back isn't my back. I'm forty-six. We live together, me and Carla, new apartment on Ridge, second floor.
[SEG0051] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): And the freeway this morning was a complete parking lot. Forty minutes, Ridge to the clinic.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Construction by the mall. One lane since forever. They should just finish the thing.
[SEG0053] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Rain all weekend too. Our grandson's T-ball will be a swamp. He's six, still runs the wrong way after the ball.
[SEG0054] person_2 (PATIENT): Last game he pulled his helmet off to wave at a dog. Coach went gray on the spot.
[SEG0055] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Team's called the Green Sox. I drew snack duty, goldfish crackers and orange slices. Don't get me started on the snack spreadsheet.
[SEG0056] person_2 (PATIENT): She has a spreadsheet. For snacks. I'm just saying.
[SEG0057] person_1 (DOCTOR): Front's moving through, it'll pass. Bend forward for me, feet together, toward the toes.
[SEG0058] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the limit. It pulls.
[SEG0059] person_1 (DOCTOR): Flexion's limited. Left paraspinal muscles are tight. This where it lives?
[SEG0060] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah. That's it. Still not a big deal.
[SEG0061] person_1 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise. Tell me if this shoots.
[SEG0062] person_2 (PATIENT): No shoot. Just a hamstring stretch, ordinary.
[SEG0063] person_1 (DOCTOR): Straight leg raise is negative both sides. Gait was normal when you walked in.
[SEG0064] person_1 (DOCTOR): Vitals from the desk, blood pressure one thirty-eight over eighty-four, heart rate seventy-two, temperature ninety-eight point six, oxygen ninety-eight percent.

[SEG0065] person_1 (DOCTOR): Working impression, mechanical low back strain. No red flags I can hang a dangerous diagnosis on. Wife's foot story, I can't fully exclude a bit of nerve irritation, but that's not my lead thought.
[SEG0066] person_2 (PATIENT): So basically I'm fine and we can wrap this.
[SEG0067] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not injured-emergency fine. No film today. If it's not clearly better in three weeks, we'll get a plain x-ray of the lumbar spine.
[SEG0068] person_1 (DOCTOR): Stay active, skip the hero lifts, ice or heat, your call. Ibuprofen with food, four hundred milligrams, one tablet, up to three times a day. Do not double after you skip.
[SEG0069] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, yeah, one tablet with food, and I won't play hero with the boxes.
[SEG0070] person_1 (DOCTOR): Physical therapy referral is going in. If you can't urinate, a leg gets weak, or a fever shows up, emergency room, not another shift.
[SEG0071] person_2 (PATIENT): Therapy, really? I'll go if Carla nags. And I heard the ER part.
[SEG0072] person_1 (DOCTOR): Come back if it's not better in three weeks. If it settles, you don't need me.
[SEG0073] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll put it on the calendar. And we're taking surface streets, I am not doing that mall backup again.
[SEG0074] person_1 (DOCTOR): Desk has the therapy slip. That's all.

spec.situation: Manual worker or office worker with low back pain for 'a few weeks or since the move'; doctor asks about red flags (numbness, bladder, weight loss, fever) one by one; patient answers some clearly, some vaguely or with a story. Painkiller use mentioned.
features: spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.
tangent_small_talk: a long tangent or small talk (traffic, cricket, the weather, a grandchild) that holds NO clinical content; nothing from it is extracted.
ambiguous_answer: an answer that sounds like yes but is really 'maybe' ('mm, I suppose', 'sometimes, not really'); recorded with uncertainty or not at all, never as a firm fact.
